## Overview

[OpenHEXA](https://github.com/BLSQ/openhexa) is an open-source data integration platform developed by
[Bluesquare](https://bluesquarehub.com). Data and analyses are organised in **workspaces**, which hold files, versioned
**datasets**, a PostgreSQL **database** with **saved queries**, **pipelines**, **web apps** and **connections** to
external systems such as DHIS2 or IASO.

The openhexa package lets you work with all of these from R: from an OpenHEXA notebook, from RStudio on your laptop,
or from a script running anywhere. You never deal with the API: you list things, select a workspace, and get data
frames back.

## Installation

The package is preinstalled in OpenHEXA notebooks. Elsewhere, install the latest release from GitHub:

```r
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("BLSQ/openhexa-sdk-r")
```

### Installing a specific version

Releases are tagged on GitHub (`v0.1.0`, `v0.2.0`, ...). R keeps a single version of a package per library, so the
version is chosen when installing:

```r
remotes::install_github("BLSQ/openhexa-sdk-r@v0.2.0")
```

To pin the version for a project, use [renv](https://rstudio.github.io/renv/): it records the version in a lockfile
that restores the same environment on another computer, or in an OpenHEXA workspace.

```r
renv::install("BLSQ/openhexa-sdk-r@v0.2.0")
renv::snapshot()
```

A script can also check the installed version:

```r
stopifnot(packageVersion("openhexa") >= "0.2.0")
```

Versions follow [semantic versioning](https://semver.org). Before 1.0.0, breaking changes increase the minor version
(0.1.x to 0.2.0), so pinning the minor version protects you from them.

## Authenticate

The package is installed in the R image of OpenHEXA notebooks, and the connection is already configured there: skip
this step. The same goes for notebook pipelines written in R, where the access is limited to the workspace of the
pipeline, for the duration of the run.

Elsewhere, generate an API token from your OpenHEXA user settings, then log in. In an interactive session, you are
prompted for the token, so that it doesn't end up in your scripts:

```{r}
library(openhexa)

login(server_url = "https://api.openhexa.org")
#> OpenHEXA API token: ****
#> ✔ Authenticated as Ada Lovelace on https://api.openhexa.org.
```

In batch mode (scheduled scripts, CI), pass the token, or set the `HEXA_SERVER_URL`, `HEXA_TOKEN` and `HEXA_WORKSPACE`
environment variables, e.g. in your `.Renviron`:

```{r}
login(token = Sys.getenv("OPENHEXA_TOKEN"), server_url = "https://api.openhexa.org")
```

## Explore

List the workspaces you have access to, and select the one to work with. Every function then uses it by default:

```{r}
list_workspaces()

set_workspace("malaria-burkina")
#> ✔ Using workspace Malaria Burkina Faso ("malaria-burkina").
```

Then list what the workspace contains:

```{r}
# datasets, including the ones shared with the workspace
list_datasets()

# files, at the root of the workspace or in a folder
list_files()
list_files("data/")

# saved queries of the Data Studio
list_saved_queries()

# web apps, pipelines and connections
list_webapps()
list_pipelines()
list_connections()
```

Every function also accepts a `workspace` argument, to work with another workspace without switching:

```{r}
list_datasets(workspace = "malaria-niger")
```

## Get data

### Files

`get_file()` reads a workspace file into R, with a reader picked from its extension: CSV, TSV, Parquet (requires
arrow), Excel (requires readxl), JSON and RDS. Inside OpenHEXA, the file is read straight from the workspace;
elsewhere, it is downloaded first.

```{r}
population <- get_file("data/population_2024.csv")

# pass a reader for other formats
districts <- get_file("data/districts.geojson", reader = sf::st_read) # requires sf
```

`download_file()` downloads a file without reading it:

```{r}
download_file("reports/annual_report.pdf", dest = "annual_report.pdf")
```

### Datasets

Datasets are versioned collections of files. Look at their versions and files, then read one file, or stack all the
tables of a version:

```{r}
get_dataset("routine-data")
list_dataset_versions("routine-data")
list_dataset_files("routine-data")

# one file, from the latest version or a given one
cases <- get_dataset_file("routine-data", "cases.parquet")
cases_q1 <- get_dataset_file("routine-data", "cases.parquet", version = "2024-Q1")

# all the tables of a version in a single data frame, with a `file` column
all_cases <- get_dataset_data("routine-data", pattern = "^cases_")
```

### Saved queries

Saved queries are SQL queries on the workspace database, written in the Data Studio. Run them to get their result as a
data frame; you don't need the database credentials:

```{r}
monthly <- run_saved_query("monthly-malaria-cases", max_rows = 10000)
```

### The workspace database

For full SQL access, connect with DBI (requires the DBI and RPostgres packages, and the permission to see the database
credentials). It works with dplyr (and dbplyr) too:

```{r}
con <- connect_database()
DBI::dbListTables(con)
dplyr::tbl(con, "cases") |>
  dplyr::filter(year == 2024) |>
  dplyr::collect()
DBI::dbDisconnect(con)
```

## Share results

### Files and datasets

```{r}
write.csv(monthly, "monthly.csv", row.names = FALSE)
upload_file("monthly.csv", "outputs/monthly.csv")

create_dataset_version("routine-data", "2024-Q4", changelog = "Q4 extraction")
add_dataset_file("routine-data", "monthly.csv")
```

### Web apps

`publish_webapp()` publishes HTML as a web app of the workspace, and returns its URL. It accepts a string of HTML, an
HTML file, a folder with an `index.html`, or any htmlwidget: plotly charts, leaflet maps, DT tables, etc.

```{r}
publish_webapp("Hello", "<h1>Hello from R</h1>")

# install.packages("plotly")
chart <- plotly::plot_ly(monthly, x = ~month, y = ~cases, color = ~district, type = "bar")
app <- publish_webapp("Malaria cases", chart, description = "Monthly cases by district")
app$url
```

Publishing again under the same name replaces the content of the web app, so the URL stays the same:

```{r}
publish_webapp("Malaria cases", "dashboard/", message = "Add Q4 data")
```

### Notebooks

`create_notebook()` creates an R notebook in the workspace, ready to be opened from the Notebooks page. Cells are code
cells, unless named `markdown`:

```{r}
create_notebook("analysis/malaria.ipynb", c(
  markdown = "# Monthly malaria cases",
  "library(openhexa)",
  "monthly <- run_saved_query('monthly-malaria-cases')",
  "summary(monthly)"
))
```

## Pipelines and connections

Look at the parameters of a pipeline, run it and wait for the result:

```{r}
get_pipeline("dhis2-extract")

run <- run_pipeline(
  "dhis2-extract",
  config = list(start_date = "2024-01-01", org_units = I("BF")),
  wait = TRUE
)
run$status
run$messages

list_pipeline_runs("dhis2-extract")
```

Connections hold the credentials of external systems, configured once at the workspace level. Secret values are
hidden when printed:

```{r}
dhis2 <- get_dhis2_connection("dhis2-burkina")
dhis2$url
```

## Going further

- `graphql_query()` runs any query against the OpenHEXA [GraphQL API](https://api.openhexa.org/graphql/), for what
  the package does not cover.
- Errors have classes (`openhexa_not_found_error`, `openhexa_permission_error`, ...), so they can be handled with
  `tryCatch()`.
- To work with several servers in the same session, build clients with `openhexa_client()` and pass them as
  `client`.
